lens: Fact and integrity audit of /home/user/livewell-land/client/public/essays/the-historical-jesus.json (updated 2026-10-28) against its claims ledger /home/user/livewell-land/docs/work/essays/ledgers/the-historical-jesus.md, the BSB chapter files in client/public/bible/ch/, the ESV copy (lguenth/mdbible, commit fd66568), the WDB clone (Eusebius NPNF, Origen ANF), Gutenberg Schweitzer 45422 and Perseus Tacitus, all already in the session scratchpad, and the integrity rules in /home/user/Livewell-/docs/work/essays/BRIEF.md. Read-only. This run used 8 of its 30 web searches on 2026-10-28; it saw search-engine summaries only and opened no page. The published body differs from docs/work/essays/the-historical-jesus.md only in dropping the title and standfirst lines and the parenthetical sentence linking Did Christianity Copy Pagan Myths?. This run rematched all 39 quoted strings: 25 Scripture quotations against the ESV copy (all match), three Schweitzer sentences against Gutenberg 45422, Tacitus against Perseus, and the Josephus/Eusebius and Celsus/Origen quotations against WDB. All match word for word.

findings.where: What Outsiders Said, second paragraph: "Josephus mentions Jesus only so his readers will know which James he means. A Christian copyist would hardly have called his Lord "the so-called Christ," and the story is about Ananus abusing his office."
findings.problem: (c) The argument depends on McGiffert's English, not on Josephus's Greek. "The so-called Christ" renders tou legomenou Christou (Ant. 20.200). Matthew, a Christian writer, uses the same participle of Jesus: "Jesus ... who is called Christ" (Matthew 1:16, ho legomenos Christos; the BSB interlinear in client/public/bible/ch/matthew/1.json shows legomenos). Pilate uses it in Matthew 27:17 and 27:22. This run's search found the counterpoint in the literature: G. A. Wells cites Matthew 1:16 against the argument, and R. T. France replies that the phrase is too noncommittal for an interpolator. A skeptic who knows Matthew 1:16 can show that the premise as worded, that a Christian would not use this phrase of his Lord, is false. The ledger records the translation choice but never tests the argument built on it. The quotation in the sentence before is accurate and stays.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "A Christian copyist would hardly have named his Lord only in passing, with so noncommittal a phrase, and the story is about Ananus abusing his office." This is paraphrase and needs no quotation marks. Add a ledger line citing Ant. 20.200 (tou legomenou Christou), Matthew 1:16, and the France and Wells exchange as this run's search summarized it.

findings.where: What Outsiders Said, second paragraph: "A Jew who never became a Christian would not have written that."
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line covers the implied claim that Josephus never became a Christian. It is supported: this run read Origen, Against Celsus 1.47, in WDB, where Origen says Josephus wrote "although not believing in Jesus as the Christ."
findings.fix: No essay change. Add a ledger line: Josephus did not become a Christian. Origen, Against Celsus 1.47 (WDB, ANF): "Now this writer, although not believing in Jesus as the Christ ..."

findings.where: The Case That Jesus Never Lived, first paragraph: "And Paul, the earliest Christian writer whose work we have, says strikingly little ..."
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line states that Paul is the earliest Christian writer whose work survives. The voice pass changed the parallel line in What Paul Knew to "older than any of the Gospels" but left this one. The claim is mainstream. Search 11 dates 1 Thessalonians to about 49 to 51. This run's search saw Wikipedia call it "one of the earliest surviving Christian texts" and Ehrman call it "quite possibly, the earliest surviving Christian text". Some scholars date Galatians earlier, but that letter is also Paul's.
findings.fix: No essay change needed. Add a ledger line citing Search 11 and this run's search. If James wants the hedge to match the sources exactly, write: "And Paul, by most scholars' dating the earliest Christian writer whose work we have, says strikingly little ..."

findings.where: What Outsiders Said, third paragraph: "If Josephus hadn't happened to tell the story, we'd never know the man existed."
findings.problem: (a) No ledger line records that Jewish War 6.5.3 is the only ancient account of Jesus son of Ananias. The claim is standard, but no run recorded checking it, and this run did not search it.
findings.fix: Keep the sentence. Add a ledger line once a source confirms that Josephus is the only ancient witness to Jesus son of Ananias. Until then, the inference rests on the absence of any other account the runs saw.

findings.where: What Historians Agree On, third paragraph: "When a man kneels and calls him "Good Teacher," Mark's Jesus answers, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18)."
findings.problem: (e) "Good Teacher" is quoted from Mark 10:17 (ESV: "a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, 'Good Teacher ...'"), but the only reference in the sentence is Mark 10:18. The wording matches the ESV, and the BSB confirms the sense.
findings.fix: Change "(Mark 10:18)" to "(Mark 10:17–18)" with an en-dash, as in "Mark 8:27–29".

findings.where: The Question Jesus Asked Peter, third paragraph: "Barton's executive doesn't need a cross, and neither does the gentle teacher of the nineteenth century, the sage of the colored beads, or the Jesus who shares our politics."
findings.problem: Internal tension, which a careful reader could take as an overstatement. Earlier, the essay's own Schweitzer passage describes the nineteenth-century Jesus as one who "died to consecrate his work" (Schweitzer: "died to give His work its final consecration"). The Jesus Seminar also accepted the crucifixion as historical. The line works as a theological judgment, that the cross bears no weight in these portraits, but read literally it contradicts the essay's own source.
findings.fix: Optional rewording: "In none of them does the cross carry any weight: not Barton's executive, not the gentle teacher of the nineteenth century, not the sage of the colored beads, and not the Jesus who shares our politics." Or leave the line as it stands if James reads it as a theological judgment.

findings.problem: (c) The ledger lists three links, including /writing/did-christianity-copy-pagan-myths. The published body has two, /writing/why-trust-the-bible and /writing/did-the-resurrection-happen. The parenthetical sentence after "That argument is modern." was removed when the essay landed. Both remaining slugs are in docs/work/essays/link-targets.json.
findings.fix: No essay change. Update the ledger: two links, and the pagan-myths sentence was removed in the landed JSON.

findings.where: Ledger, "The quests and the inventions": the best-seller line ("topped the nonfiction bestseller list" on publication in 1925)
findings.problem: (c) This run's search saw Lithub's list of annual nonfiction best-sellers put The Man Nobody Knows fourth in 1925, behind Diet and Health, and first in 1926. Wikipedia says it topped the list when published. The essay's sentence ("It went to the top of the nonfiction best-seller list") gives no year, so it stays true. The ledger's "on publication in 1925" gloss is not secure.
findings.fix: No essay change. Do not add a year to the best-seller sentence. In the ledger, record that it was the top nonfiction title of 1926 and fourth in 1925 on Lithub's annual list, with Wikipedia's "topped the list when published" as the softer account.

findings.where: What Historians Agree On, fourth paragraph: "Near the start of his book *Jesus and Judaism*, E. P. Sanders ..."
findings.problem: (g) The writer's original was "his 1985 book *Jesus and Judaism*". The voice pass dropped the year to thin the title-and-year citations, not for lack of a source, and Search 36 confirms 1985. It is a restoration candidate in form only: the BRIEF says to give a year only when it matters, and the restoration rule exists to undo integrity-driven generalizations. That is why this is "consider", not "should".
findings.fix: Optional. Only if James wants the date: "Near the start of his 1985 book *Jesus and Judaism*, E. P. Sanders ..." Otherwise leave it.

clean_checks: Scripture, (e): all 25 quotations match the ESV copy word for word (rematched by script in this run): Galatians 4:4; Romans 1:3; 1 Corinthians 11:23; Galatians 1:19 (twice); 1 Corinthians 9:5; Mark 6:3; Mark 3:21; Mark 3:22 (two parts); Matthew 3:14; Mark 13:32; Mark 10:17 and 10:18; Matthew 19:17; Deuteronomy 21:23; 1 Corinthians 1:23; Mark 8:27, 8:28, 8:29 (two parts); Mark 8:33; Acts 26:26; John 1:46 (two parts); Hebrews 13:8. Each reference was read in the BSB chapter files and matches the verse's sense and its speaker: Nathanael and Philip; the scribes from Jerusalem; Paul before Agrippa; Jesus' family in Mark 3:21; Galatians 1:18 for the first Jerusalem visit; Galatians 2:9 for James as a pillar. Nested single quotation marks in Matthew 3:14 and Mark 3:21 are correct. Both Closing Texts are in the BRIEF's *"Quote."* (Reference) form.

Josephus quotations, (d): "brought before them the brother of Jesus, the so-called Christ, James by name, together with some others," matches WDB Eusebius 2.23.22 (McGiffert). "a wise man, if indeed it be proper to call him a man," and "He was the Christ." match WDB Eusebius 1.11.7. The comma placement inside the closing quotation marks is American convention, not a wording change.

Tacitus quotation, (d): matches Perseus Church and Brodribb, Annals 15.44, word for word. The source runs on ("again broke out not only in Judaea"), and the essay closes the quotation with a comma inside the marks, which is convention. The paraphrase "spreading from Judea to Rome itself" matches the next clause.

Celsus quotations, (d): "invented his birth from a virgin" and "born in a certain Jewish village, of a poor woman of the country, who gained her subsistence by spinning" match WDB Origen, Against Celsus 1.28 (ANF). The paraphrase (carpenter husband, adultery, servant in Egypt, miraculous powers, proclaimed himself a god) matches the same passage.

Schweitzer quotations, (d): "each individual created Him in accordance with his own character.", "There is no historical task which so reveals a man's true self as the writing of a Life of Jesus." and "He is a figure designed by rationalism, endowed with life by liberalism, and clothed by modern theology in an historical garb." were found verbatim in Gutenberg 45422 (Montgomery) in this run. "Founded the Kingdom of Heaven upon earth" supports the essay's "kingdom of heaven".

Barton quotation, (d): "picked up twelve men from the bottom ranks of business and forged them into an organization that conquered the world." This run's search saw Christian History Institute, Wikipedia and Encyclopedia.com give the same wording for the 1925 book; the restoration run's 1926 Spectator review (R13) supports the first half. The 1925 printing has still not been opened, which the ledger records honestly. Advertising executive, 1925, and Jesus as founder of modern business are all confirmed.

Berlin, 1910: January 31 and February 1, Zoological Garden, German Monist League. Confirmed again by this run's search, which saw the proceedings title quoted in Church History. "Two-day" is right. This run's search, like the restoration run's, found nothing on evening sessions, so "two-night" correctly stays out. Drews (Karlsruhe, professor of philosophy; Die Christusmythe 1909), Bruno Bauer, "from city to city" (Warfield, R24) and the controversy of 1909 to 1913 all match their ledger lines.

Barna: 2015 release, 92 percent, and 87 percent among Millennials, the youngest of four generations (96, 95, 91, 87). This run's search confirmed it again on barna.org and the bciowa.org reprint. "Published ... in 2015" correctly avoids dating the 2014 fieldwork.

Missing evidence (no document, inscription, coin, letter or trial record; no writings of his own), Mark around 70, "some forty years", Paul's letters in the 50s at "some twenty to twenty-five years", Pilate's ten years in Judea and the one stone inscription: all match ledger lines with sources.

Carrier (living): On the Historicity of Jesus, 2014, Sheffield Phoenix Press, Bayesian method, celestial Jesus, his reading of "the Lord's brother", and his concession of the expert consensus. This run's search saw Carrier call historicity the "near-universal consensus of well-qualified experts" and describe mythicism as a fringe position. The essay's characterization is fair and unloaded. (f) clean.

Ehrman (living): agnostic; Did Jesus Exist? (2012), written against the mythicists; his conclusion of a Jewish preacher crucified under Pilate in Tiberius's reign. All in the ledger. "One of the best-known New Testament scholars in America" has no separate ledger line but is a generous, uncontroversial description. (f) clean.

Richard Hays: this run's search confirms he died on January 3, 2025, so he is not a living person. The sentence about him is paraphrase without quotation marks and is supported by his 2010 remark ("It was a self-selected group of scholars who held a particular view"). Robert Funk (d. 2005) and E. P. Sanders (d. 2022) are not living either.

Josephus biography (priest's son, Galilee command, went over to the Romans, settled in Rome), Antiquities Book 20 finished in the 90s (93/94), Ananus between Festus's death and Albinus's arrival around 62, most historians accepting the James passage, and many specialists favoring a shorter original Testimonium: all match the ledger and the sources the runs saw.

Jesus son of Ananias (War 6.5.3): about four years before the revolt; leading men beat him; the rulers handed him to Albinus; flogged to the bone; released as a madman; killed by a stone from a siege engine. All match Perseus Whiston via the ledger. "Roman" is a sound inference from the Roman siege.
Tacitus early in the second century, the fire of 64, Nero blaming the Christians, Tacitus's contempt for them, and the skeptics' objection (Carrier): all in the ledger with sources.

Celsus: second century; the first pagan attack on Christianity at length that we know of; survives inside Origen; the Jewish critic; and no ancient opponent denying that Jesus existed (Volney and Dupuis as the first, eighteenth century). All in the ledger.

Gospel evidence: Mark and Matthew name John as the baptizer and Luke does not; John's baptism was one of repentance; Mark 3:21; Mark 13:32; Mark 10:18 against Matthew 19:17; crucifixion as the death of slaves and rebels; the crucifixion as the firmest fact. All match.

Sanders's list (Jesus and Judaism, p. 11): baptism, Galilean preacher and healer, the twelve, Israel only, temple controversy, crucifixion by Roman authorities, a continuing movement, some persecution. It matches the eight items and is unquoted paraphrase. His standing and the historians' additions (kingdom, parables, healer and exorcist) are in the ledger.

Reimarus and Lessing (1774 to 1778, Hamburg, a failed political messiah), the nineteenth-century lives of Jesus, Schweitzer in Strasbourg in 1906 at about 31, and Schweitzer's own eschatological Jesus: all match Gutenberg Schweitzer via the ledger.

Sallman: Head of Christ (1940); light skin, long brown hair, soft lighting; the Salvation Army and the YMCA giving pocket copies to American soldiers in the Second World War; "by some estimates" more than half a billion reproductions by century's end. All match R20 and R21.

Jesus Seminar: Robert Funk, 1985; red and black beads; The Five Gospels (1993); most sayings judged inauthentic (about 18 percent judged authentic); a sage with little apocalyptic preaching. All match.

Caesarea Philippi north of the Sea of Galilee, the paraphrase of Mark 8:31-33, the Apostles' Creed ("suffered under Pontius Pilate", between the virgin birth and the resurrection, matching the site creed), and Acts 26 before Agrippa: all match.

Restorations, (g): all eight entries under "Original wording, for restoring" are restored in the published text as the ledger describes (date and venue, city to city, both Barna figures, the three Schweitzer sentences, Barton and the best-seller line, Sallman, Hays). None is still pending. "Deceiver", which the voice pass cut without checking, is not proposed: it would rebuild a triplet the BRIEF warns against.

Mechanics: no em-dash (U+2014). One en-dash, in the verse range Mark 8:27–29. The only exclamation point is inside quoted Mark 8:33. None of the CLAUDE.md forbidden words or phrases appears, and neither do "fair" nor "honest". Both links are in link-targets.json. No biography of James beyond the first-person confession; no contested second-order question argued.

Excerpt: "Nearly every historian of the ancient world, believer or not, agrees that Jesus of Nazareth lived and was crucified under Pontius Pilate" is supported by Search 34 ("virtually all scholars of antiquity").
